los.text: Identify key outcomes from clinical history, examination & initial investigations in a child with suspected malabsorption
los.html:
History
  • Stool pattern (chronic diarrhoea, pale, bulky, offensive, floating = steatorrhoea)
  • Abdominal distension/bloating
  • Pain
  • Vomiting
  • Irritability
  • Faltering growth/weight loss
  • Appetite
  • Timing relative to gluten introduction (coeliac) or cow's milk
  • Recurrent chest infections (CF)
  • Dietary history
  • FHx (coeliac, CF, IBD, T1DM, autoimmune thyroid)
  • Travel/infection (Giardia)
  • Developmental history
  • Safeguarding (neglect).
Examination
  • Growth chart (weight then height crossing centiles; BMI)
  • Wasting (thin limbs, buttocks)
  • Abdominal distension
  • Pallor (anaemia)
  • Oedema (hypoalbuminaemia)
  • Clubbing (CF, Crohn's)
  • Mouth ulcers
  • Perianal disease (Crohn's)
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis
  • Rickets/vitamin deficiency signs
  • Chest signs (CF)
  • Delayed puberty.
Initial investigations
  • FBC (iron-deficiency/macrocytic anaemia)
  • Ferritin, folate, B12
  • U&E, LFT, albumin
  • CRP/ESR
  • Calcium
  • Vitamin D
  • Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA)
  • TFTs
  • Stool: microscopy/culture/Giardia
  • Faecal elastase (pancreatic insufficiency)
  • Faecal calprotectin (IBD)
  • Sweat test (CF)
  • Urine culture
  • Clotting (vitamin K).
Key outcomes to identify
  • Degree of growth failure
  • Evidence of malabsorption (fat/protein/micronutrient)
  • Likely cause (coeliac commonest; CF; cow's milk protein allergy; IBD; Giardia; short gut)
  • Complications
  • and need for specialist referral (endoscopy/biopsy, dietitian).

los.text: Know the causes, investigation and overview of medical management of chronic constipation
los.html:
Definition (Rome IV)≥2 of: straining, lumpy/hard stools (Bristol 1–2), incomplete evacuation, sensation of obstruction, manual manoeuvres, <3 BMs/week, for ≥3 months.
Causes
  • Primary/functional: slow transit, dyssynergic defaecation (pelvic floor), IBS-C.
  • Secondary: drugs (opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium channel blockers (verapamil), antacids (aluminium), TCAs, antipsychotics, ondansetron), low fibre/fluid, immobility, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, diabetes (autonomic neuropathy), neurological (Parkinson's, MS, spinal cord injury), colorectal cancer, strictures, anal fissure (pain avoidance), pregnancy, depression.
Red flags(→ 2WW/colonoscopy)Age >50 with new change, rectal bleeding, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal/rectal mass, FHx bowel cancer/IBD, positive FIT.
Investigations
  • Usually clinical
  • FBC, Ca²⁺, TFTs, glucose, coeliac serology
  • FIT if symptoms
  • Colonoscopy/CT colonography if red flags
  • Specialist: transit studies (radio-opaque markers), anorectal manometry, defaecating proctography.
Overview of management
  • Lifestyle (fibre ~30 g/day, fluids, exercise, toilet routine/positioning with footstool)
  • Stop constipating drugs
  • Laxatives stepwise (bulk-forming → osmotic (macrogol) → stimulant)
  • Prucalopride/linaclotide if refractory
  • Biofeedback for dyssynergia
  • Treat faecal impaction (macrogol disimpaction regimen ± enemas)
  • Surgery rarely.

los.text: Appraise different drugs for constipation, and contrast their mechanism of action.
los.html:
ClassExamplesMechanismNotes
Bulk-formingIspaghula husk (Fybogel), methylcellulose, sterculiaRetain water → ↑ stool mass → stimulates peristalsisTakes 2–3 days; need adequate fluid (obstruction risk); bloating; not for opioid-induced
OsmoticMacrogol (polyethylene glycol, Laxido/Movicol), lactulose, magnesium salts, phosphate enemasRetain water in lumen by osmosisMacrogol: first-line in many (also disimpaction, children). Lactulose: bloating/flatulence (colonic fermentation), used in hepatic encephalopathy (↓ ammonia)
StimulantSenna, bisacodyl, sodium picosulfate, docusate (also softener), glycerol suppositories↑ colonic motility (enteric nerve stimulation) and secretionCramps; opioid-induced constipation (with softener); avoid in obstruction
SoftenersDocusate, arachis oil enemaLower surface tension; lubricateArachis oil: peanut allergy
SecretagoguesLinaclotide (guanylate cyclase-C agonist), lubiprostone (ClC-2 activator)↑ intestinal fluid secretion (↑ cGMP → CFTR)IBS-C / chronic constipation; diarrhoea
ProkineticPrucalopride5-HT4 agonist → ↑ colonic motilityChronic constipation in women when laxatives fail
PAMORAsNaloxegol, methylnaltrexone, naldemedinePeripherally acting μ-opioid antagonists (don't cross BBB)Opioid-induced constipation without reversing analgesia
  • Choose: by cause, onset speed needed, patient factors (renal: avoid Mg/phosphate; elderly), and route (oral vs rectal for impaction).

los.text: Link diseases of the large bowel to signs, symptoms, investigations and likely diagnoses.
sessions: Pathology of large bowel and appendix
los.html:
DiseaseSymptoms/signsInvestigationsDiagnosis
Colorectal adenocarcinomaChange in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia (right-sided: often anaemia only), mass, obstruction, weight lossFIT, colonoscopy + biopsy, CT colonography, staging CT, CEAAdenocarcinoma (Dukes/TNM)
Diverticular disease/diverticulitisLIF pain, fever, tenderness, change in habit, PR bleeding (painless, large)CRP/WCC, CT abdomen (acute), colonoscopy laterDiverticulitis ± abscess/perforation
Ulcerative colitis / Crohn's colitisBloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmusCalprotectin, colonoscopy + biopsiesIBD
Infective colitis (incl. C. difficile)Diarrhoea ± blood, fever, recent antibioticsStool culture, C. diff toxin
Ischaemic colitisElderly, vascular disease; sudden LIF pain + bloody diarrhoea (watershed areas: splenic flexure)CT, colonoscopy ("thumbprinting")
Microscopic colitisChronic watery diarrhoea, older women, NSAIDs/PPIs/SSRIsNormal colonoscopy, biopsies (collagenous/lymphocytic)Budesonide
AppendicitisPeriumbilical → RIF pain, anorexia, fever, rebound/guarding, Rovsing'sClinical, WCC/CRP, USS (children/women), CT
Volvulus (sigmoid, caecal)Distension, absolute constipation, vomitingAXR (coffee bean), CT
Haemorrhoids, fissureBright red bleeding on paper; painful defaecation (fissure)PR/proctoscopy
AngiodysplasiaElderly, painless bleeding/anaemia (aortic stenosis: Heyde's)Colonoscopy, CT angiography
Polyps
  • Hyperplastic (benign), adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, villous: risk ↑ with size >1 cm, villous component, high-grade dysplasia), sessile serrated lesions (serrated pathway)
  • FAP (APC; hundreds of polyps), Lynch (MMR genes; right-sided cancers).
Bowel screening (Wales)FIT every 2 years, ages 50–74 (Bowel Screening Wales).

los.text: Identify the large intestine, appendix and link them to function and likely pathology.
sessions: Pathology of large bowel and appendix
los.html:
Large intestine (~1.5 m)
  • Caecum (RIF, with appendix and ileocaecal valve)
  • → ascending colon (retroperitoneal)
  • → hepatic flexure
  • → transverse colon (intraperitoneal, mesentery)
  • → splenic flexure
  • → descending (retroperitoneal)
  • → sigmoid (intraperitoneal, sigmoid mesocolon)
  • → rectum
  • → anal canal.
Features
  • Taeniae coli (3 longitudinal muscle bands; converge at appendix base), haustra (sacculations), appendices epiploicae (fat tags)
  • No villi
  • Crypts rich in goblet cells.
Function
  • Water and electrolyte absorption (~1.5 L/day; Na⁺ via ENaC, K⁺ secretion)
  • Storage and elimination of faeces
  • Bacterial fermentation (short-chain fatty acids, vitamin K)
  • Mucus secretion.
Appendix
  • Blind-ended tube from posteromedial caecum
  • Lymphoid tissue (GALT)
  • Base at McBurney's point (⅓ from ASIS to umbilicus)
  • Appendicular artery (from ileocolic, end artery → gangrene/perforation when obstructed).
Link to pathology
  • Right colon (wide, liquid stool) → cancers present with anaemia/mass
  • Left colon (narrow, solid stool) → obstruction, change in habit
  • Sigmoid (high pressure) → diverticula and volvulus (long mesentery)
  • Watershed areas (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid) → ischaemic colitis
  • Caecum (widest) → perforation risk in distal obstruction (Laplace)
  • Appendix (lumen obstruction by faecolith/lymphoid hyperplasia) → appendicitis
  • Carcinoid tumours.
Histology identificationColon (straight tubular crypts, many goblet cells, no villi), appendix (lymphoid follicles in mucosa/submucosa, small lumen).

los.text: Formulate a definition and appraise common presenting symptoms of IBS
los.html:
Definition (Rome IV)
  • Recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week in the last 3 months
  • with ≥2 of: related to defaecation
  • Associated with change in stool frequency
  • Associated with change in stool form
  • Onset ≥6 months before diagnosis.
  • Disorder of gut–brain interaction.
NICE diagnostic approach
  • Consider IBS if ≥6 months of abdominal pain/discomfort, bloating or change in bowel habit
  • Diagnose if pain is relieved by defaecation or associated with altered frequency/form
  • Plus ≥2 of: altered stool passage (straining, urgency, incomplete evacuation)
  • Bloating/distension
  • Symptoms worse with eating
  • Passage of mucus.
SubtypesIBS-C (constipation), IBS-D (diarrhoea), IBS-M (mixed), unclassified.
Common symptomsCrampy pain, bloating, altered habit, urgency, mucus, incomplete evacuation; extraintestinal: fatigue, nausea, backache, urinary symptoms, dyspareunia; associated anxiety/depression, fibromyalgia.
Epidemiology~10–20% prevalence; women > men; onset typically <50.
PathophysiologyVisceral hypersensitivity, altered motility, microbiome changes, post-infectious, low-grade inflammation, stress/psychological factors, central sensitisation.
AppraisalPositive diagnosis after limited tests (don't over-investigate); symptoms overlap with coeliac, IBD, bile acid diarrhoea, microscopic colitis, ovarian cancer.

los.text: Assess potential red flags in IBS symptoms and judge when to initiate investigations for more serious disorders
los.html:
Red flags (refer/investigate)
  • Age >50 (new symptoms) / change in habit after 60
  • Rectal bleeding
  • Unexplained weight loss
  • Iron-deficiency anaemia
  • Nocturnal symptoms (pain/diarrhoea waking from sleep)
  • Abdominal or rectal mass
  • FHx of bowel or ovarian cancer
  • IBD or coeliac
  • Fever
  • Persistent diarrhoea
  • Raised inflammatory markers
  • Positive FIT
  • Short history/progressive symptoms.
WomenPersistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain, urinary symptoms (especially ≥50) → CA-125 (ovarian cancer), pelvic USS if raised.
Baseline tests in suspected IBS (NICE)
  • FBC, ESR/CRP, coeliac serology (tTG)
  • Faecal calprotectin (to exclude IBD in <40s with diarrhoea)
  • CA-125 if indicated.
  • Not needed routinely: USS, colonoscopy, TFTs, stool cultures, hydrogen breath tests.
When to investigate further
  • Red flags (2WW colonoscopy/CT)
  • Abnormal tests (↑ calprotectin → colonoscopy; +ve coeliac → endoscopy/biopsy)
  • Atypical features
  • Failure of treatment
  • Bile acid diarrhoea (SeHCAT scan) if IBS-D refractory
  • Microscopic colitis (older, NSAIDs/PPIs).
JudgementBalance missing organic disease vs harms/cost/anxiety of over-investigation; make a positive diagnosis and explain it.

los.text: Examine the lifestyle and dietary management of irritable bowel syndrome, including the FODMAP diet.
los.html:
First-line lifestyle/diet (NICE/BDA)
  • Regular meals, take time to eat, avoid skipping meals or eating late.
  • Fluids: ≥8 cups/day (water/non-caffeinated); limit tea/coffee (≤3/day), alcohol, fizzy drinks.
  • Fibre: reduce insoluble fibre (bran) if diarrhoea/bloating; soluble fibre (oats, linseed 1 tbsp/day, ispaghula) helps constipation and bloating.
  • Limit resistant starch (processed foods), fresh fruit to 3 portions/day.
  • Diarrhoea: avoid sorbitol (sugar-free sweets/gum).
  • Physical activity, sleep, stress management.
  • Probiotics: trial for 4 weeks (limited evidence).
Second-line: low-FODMAP diet(dietitian-led)
  • FODMAPs = Fermentable Oligosaccharides (fructans: wheat, onion, garlic; GOS: legumes), Disaccharides (lactose), Monosaccharides (excess fructose: apples, honey), And Polyols (sorbitol, mannitol: stone fruits, sweeteners).
  • Mechanism: poorly absorbed short-chain carbohydrates → osmotic water drawn into small bowel + rapid colonic fermentation → gas → distension and pain in hypersensitive gut.
  • Three phases: restriction (2–6 weeks) → reintroduction (systematic challenge to identify triggers) → personalisation (long-term liberal diet).
  • Evidence: ~50–75% symptom improvement; risks: nutritional inadequacy, altered microbiome (↓ bifidobacteria), eating disorder risk → needs dietitian, avoid long-term strict restriction.
Psychological therapiesCBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy, psychological therapy if refractory >12 months.

los.text: Know the commonly used drugs for IBS and their mechanism of action, and differentiate the symptoms each is used to treat.
los.html:
DrugMechanismSymptom targeted
Antispasmodics: mebeverine, alverine, hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan), peppermint oilDirect smooth muscle relaxants (mebeverine, peppermint: Ca²⁺ channel block) / antimuscarinic (hyoscine)Pain, cramping, bloating
LoperamidePeripheral μ-opioid agonist → ↓ motility, ↑ transit time, ↑ anal toneDiarrhoea, urgency (IBS-D)
Laxatives (ispaghula, macrogol; avoid lactulose: bloating)Bulk/osmoticConstipation (IBS-C)
LinaclotideGuanylate cyclase-C agonist → ↑ secretion; ↓ visceral pain afferentsIBS-C (moderate–severe, ≥12 months, failed laxatives)
Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline 5–10 mg at night, titrate to 30 mg)Neuromodulator: ↓ visceral hypersensitivity, central pain processing, anticholinergic slowing of transitPain (second line), especially IBS-D; ATLANTIS trial (2023) supports GP use
SSRIs (citalopram)Neuromodulator; may speed transitPain (if TCA ineffective), IBS-C
Rifaximin, eluxadoline, ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist), bile acid sequestrantsVariousSpecialist/off-label: IBS-D with bloating/diarrhoea
  • Approach: target predominant symptom; review effect at ~3 months; explain neuromodulators are not used as antidepressants here.

los.text: Describe the physiology and biochemistry of refeeding
los.html:
Refeeding syndromePotentially fatal shifts in fluids and electrolytes when nutrition (oral, enteral or parenteral) is restarted after starvation/significant undernutrition.
Physiology during starvation
  • Insulin ↓, glucagon ↑
  • Body shifts from carbohydrate to fat and protein catabolism (ketones as fuel)
  • Intracellular electrolytes (phosphate, K⁺, Mg²⁺) depleted while serum levels may stay normal
  • Thiamine stores depleted
  • Basal metabolic rate ↓.
On refeeding
  • Carbohydrate
  • → ↑ insulin
  • → cellular uptake of glucose with phosphate, K⁺, Mg²⁺ (glycolysis, ATP and 2,3-BPG synthesis, glycogen, protein synthesis)
  • → hypophosphataemia (hallmark), hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia
  • Thiamine consumption → Wernicke's encephalopathy
  • Insulin → Na⁺ and water retention → fluid overload, oedema, heart failure
  • Hyperglycaemia.
Consequences↓ ATP → respiratory muscle weakness/failure, cardiac arrhythmias, heart failure, rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis, seizures, confusion, death.
High risk (NICE CG32)
  • BMI <16, unintentional weight loss >15% in 3–6 months, little/no intake >10 days, low K⁺/PO₄/Mg²⁺ before feeding
  • or ≥2 of: BMI <18.5, weight loss >10%, little intake >5 days, alcohol misuse or drugs (insulin, chemotherapy, antacids, diuretics).
  • Groups: anorexia nervosa, alcohol dependence, cancer, elderly, post-op, prolonged fasting, malabsorption.
Prevention/management
  • Check U&E, PO₄, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, glucose before and daily
  • Start low (5–10 kcal/kg/day; max ~10 kcal/kg in high risk), increase slowly over 4–7 days
  • Thiamine + vitamin B co-strong + multivitamin before and during
  • Replace K⁺, PO₄, Mg²⁺ (oral/IV)
  • Fluid balance, cardiac monitoring if severe
  • Dietitian-led.

los.text: Recognise the risk factors, signs and symptoms of eating disorders, and identify appropriate management options
los.html:
Disorders
  • Anorexia nervosa (restriction, significantly low weight, intense fear of weight gain, body image disturbance; restrictive or binge–purge type)
  • Bulimia nervosa (binge eating + compensatory behaviours (vomiting, laxatives, exercise) ≥weekly, normal/high weight)
  • Binge eating disorder (commonest; no compensation)
  • ARFID (avoidant/restrictive food intake, not body-image driven)
  • OSFED.
Risk factors
  • Female
  • Adolescence/young adulthood
  • FHx (eating disorders, depression, substance misuse)
  • Perfectionism
  • Low self-esteem
  • Anxiety/OCD
  • Dieting
  • Weight-related teasing
  • Sports emphasising weight (gymnastics, dance, running)
  • Social media/cultural thin ideal
  • Childhood adversity/abuse
  • T1DM (insulin omission: "diabulimia")
  • Autism
  • LGBTQ+.
Signs and symptoms
  • Anorexia: weight loss, amenorrhoea, cold intolerance, bradycardia, hypotension (postural), hypothermia, lanugo hair, dry skin, dizziness, fatigue, constipation, osteoporosis, delayed puberty/growth; behaviours: restricting, excessive exercise, secrecy.
  • Bulimia: Russell's sign (calluses on knuckles), parotid enlargement, dental erosion, hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (vomiting), arrhythmias, oesophageal tears.
Risk assessment (MEED guidance, 2022)
  • BMI (%median BMI in children)
  • Rate of weight loss
  • HR (<40 high risk)
  • BP/postural drop
  • Temperature
  • ECG (QTc)
  • Bloods (U&E, PO₄, Mg²⁺, glucose, FBC, LFT)
  • SUSS test (muscle power)
  • Suicidal ideation.
Management (NICE NG69)
  • Early referral to specialist eating disorder services
  • Anorexia: adults: CBT-ED, MANTRA, SSCM
  • Children/young people: family therapy (FT-AN)
  • Bulimia: guided self-help → CBT-ED
  • Children: family therapy (FT-BN)
  • BED: guided self-help, CBT-ED.
  • Medical monitoring, dietetics, refeeding risk, vitamin/mineral supplements, bone health
  • Medication not primary (SSRIs for comorbidity; lisdexamfetamine for BED off-label).
  • Admission for medical instability
  • Mental Health Act can authorise feeding as treatment for mental disorder.

los.text: Know the mechanics of PEG placement, the indications and relevant ethics
los.html:
PEG (percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy)Feeding tube through abdominal wall into stomach for long-term enteral nutrition (>4 weeks).
Mechanics ("pull" technique)
  • Patient fasted, IV prophylactic antibiotic (co-amoxiclav or as per local), sedation
  • Gastroscopy
  • → insufflate stomach
  • → transillumination and finger indentation identify site (usually left upper quadrant)
  • → local anaesthetic
  • → trocar/needle through skin into stomach
  • → guidewire passed, grasped by endoscope snare
  • → pulled out of mouth
  • → tube attached and pulled back through oesophagus and stomach out of abdominal wall
  • → internal bumper sits against gastric wall, external fixator.
  • Check position endoscopically.
  • Feeding usually starts after ~4 h (local protocol).
  • Alternatives: RIG (radiologically inserted, e.g. MND with poor respiratory function), surgical gastrostomy, NG/NJ tubes (short term), PEJ.
Indications
  • Neurological dysphagia (stroke not recovering, MND, MS, Parkinson's, cerebral palsy)
  • Head and neck cancer (before/during radiotherapy)
  • Oesophageal obstruction (if passable)
  • Long-term inadequate oral intake (CF, Crohn's, some children)
  • Gastric decompression (malignant obstruction: venting PEG).
ContraindicationsLimited life expectancy (e.g. advanced dementia), uncorrected coagulopathy, ascites, previous gastric surgery, inability to transilluminate, peritonitis, gastric outlet obstruction (feeding).
ComplicationsAspiration, peristomal infection, buried bumper, leakage, tube blockage/displacement, peritonitis (early dislodgement), bleeding, perforation, pain; procedure mortality; refeeding syndrome.
Ethics
  • Artificial nutrition is medical treatment (can be withheld/withdrawn: Bland 1993)
  • Advanced dementia: PEG doesn't improve survival, aspiration or pressure sores → "careful hand feeding" / risk feeding preferred
  • Capacity and consent
  • Best interests (MCA, consult family/LPA, IMCA)
  • Advance decisions
  • Patient's wishes and values
  • Quality of life
  • Burdens vs benefits
  • Timing in MND (before respiratory decline)
  • Withdrawing vs withholding
  • Resource considerations
  • MDT (nutrition team, SALT, dietitian).

los.text: Link the aetiopathogenesis, common presentations and management of coeliac disease.
los.html:
Aetiopathogenesis
  • Immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten (gliadin in wheat, rye, barley) in genetically susceptible people: HLA-DQ2 (~90%) / DQ8.
  • Tissue transglutaminase (tTG) deamidates gliadin peptides
  • → bind DQ2/DQ8 with high affinity
  • → CD4 T-cell response (IFN-γ) + intraepithelial lymphocytes (IL-15)
  • → villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, ↑ IELs (Marsh classification)
  • Autoantibodies to tTG and endomysium (EMA).
  • Mostly proximal small bowel (duodenum, jejunum).
AssociationsT1DM, autoimmune thyroid disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, IgA deficiency, Down/Turner syndromes, FHx (first-degree relatives ~10%), primary biliary cholangitis.
Presentations
  • GI (chronic diarrhoea/steatorrhoea, bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, constipation, IBS-like)
  • Iron-deficiency anaemia (commonest extraintestinal; also folate/B12)
  • Faltering growth/short stature/delayed puberty (children)
  • Fatigue
  • Weight loss
  • Osteoporosis
  • Mouth ulcers
  • Abnormal LFTs
  • Neuropathy/ataxia
  • Infertility/recurrent miscarriage
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces: elbows, knees, buttocks)
  • Many asymptomatic (screen at-risk groups).
Diagnosis
  • While eating gluten (≥6 weeks): tTG-IgA + total IgA (IgA deficiency → IgG-based tests) → EMA
  • Duodenal biopsies (≥4 from D2 + bulb) for adults.
  • Children: no-biopsy route if tTG ≥10× ULN + positive EMA in separate sample (ESPGHAN).
  • HLA typing to rule out (negative predictive value).
Management
  • Lifelong strict gluten-free diet (dietitian; oats usually OK if uncontaminated; Coeliac UK)
  • Annual review (symptoms, weight, tTG to monitor adherence, FBC, ferritin, folate, B12, vitamin D, calcium)
  • DEXA if risk
  • Pneumococcal vaccine (hyposplenism)
  • Screen relatives
  • Treat deficiencies.
  • Refractory → re-assess adherence, refractory coeliac disease.
ComplicationsAnaemia, osteoporosis, enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, small bowel adenocarcinoma, oesophageal SCC (risks reduce with GFD).

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of parenteral nutrition and electrolyte replacement preparations and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
Parenteral nutrition (PN)
  • IV delivery of nutrients when the GI tract is non-functional, inaccessible or inadequate (intestinal failure: short bowel, high-output fistula, prolonged ileus, obstruction, severe mucositis, severe malabsorption).
  • "If the gut works, use it": enteral preferred (cheaper, safer, maintains gut barrier).
Components ("all-in-one" bags)
  • Amino acids (protein, nitrogen)
  • Glucose (main energy, ~50–60% non-protein calories)
  • Lipid emulsion (soya/olive/fish oil; essential fatty acids, energy-dense)
  • Electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻)
  • Trace elements (zinc, selenium, copper, manganese)
  • Vitamins (water- and fat-soluble)
  • Water.
Requirements (approx., NICE CG32)Energy 25–35 kcal/kg/day (lower if critically ill/refeeding risk), protein 0.8–1.5 g/kg/day, fluid 30–35 mL/kg/day, Na⁺/K⁺ ~1 mmol/kg/day.
RouteCentral line (PICC, tunnelled CVC; hyperosmolar solutions) or peripheral PN (short term, low osmolality).
Complications
  • Line infection/CRBSI (Candida, staph)
  • Line thrombosis
  • Refeeding syndrome
  • Hyperglycaemia
  • Electrolyte disturbance
  • Fluid overload
  • PN-associated liver disease (IFALD) (cholestasis, steatosis)
  • Gallstones
  • Metabolic bone disease
  • Fatty acid/micronutrient deficiencies.
Monitoring
  • Daily U&E, glucose (capillary 4–6-hourly initially), PO₄, Mg²⁺
  • LFTs, FBC, CRP, triglycerides (lipid clearance), weight and fluid balance
  • Nutrition team (MDT).
Electrolyte replacement preparations
  • Potassium: oral (Sando-K, Kay-Cee-L) if mild; IV KCl premixed bags (e.g. 40 mmol in 1 L 0.9% NaCl); max 10 mmol/h peripherally (higher via central line with cardiac monitoring); never bolus.
  • Magnesium: oral (Mg glycerophosphate: diarrhoea) or IV MgSO₄ (e.g. 20 mmol over 12–24 h; faster in arrhythmia/eclampsia).
  • Phosphate: oral (Phosphate Sandoz: diarrhoea) or IV (Phosphates Polyfusor, glycophos) for <0.32 mmol/L or symptomatic; caution in renal failure/hypercalcaemia.
  • Calcium: IV calcium gluconate 10% (hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia cardioprotection); oral Adcal-D3.
  • Sodium: 0.9% saline; hypertonic saline (1.8%/2.7%) for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (specialist).

los.text: Identify the mechanism and site of nutrient digestion and absorption in the GIT and how common diseases affect these functions.
sessions: Digestion and absorption per GI tract region
los.html:
SiteDigestion/absorptionDiseases affecting it
MouthSalivary amylase, lingual lipase, masticationDental disease, xerostomia
StomachPepsin (protein), HCl, gastric lipase, intrinsic factor; absorbs alcohol, aspirinAtrophic gastritis/pernicious anaemia (↓ IF → B12), gastrectomy (B12, iron, dumping), PPIs (↓ B12, Mg, iron)
DuodenumPancreatic enzymes + bile; iron (Fe²⁺ via DMT1), calcium, folate startsCoeliac (iron-deficiency anaemia), duodenal resection, pancreatic insufficiency (CF, chronic pancreatitis → steatorrhoea, ADEK deficiency)
JejunumMost carbohydrate, protein, fat, folate, water-soluble vitamins; brush-border enzymes (lactase etc.)Coeliac (folate deficiency), lactase deficiency, SIBO, Crohn's
Terminal ileumVitamin B12–IF complex (cubilin receptor), bile salts (enterohepatic circulation)Crohn's, ileal resection (B12 deficiency, bile acid diarrhoea, fat malabsorption, gallstones, oxalate stones), TB, radiation
ColonWater, Na⁺, short-chain fatty acids (fermentation), vitamin KColitis (diarrhoea), colectomy (dehydration, high stoma output)
MacronutrientPathway
CarbohydrateAmylase → brush-border disaccharidases → SGLT1/GLUT5 → GLUT2
ProteinPepsin → trypsin etc. → peptidases → amino acid transporters/PepT1
FatBile emulsification → lipase → micelles → chylomicrons → lymph
  • Disease patterns: mucosal (coeliac, Crohn's)
    • luminal/maldigestion (pancreatic insufficiency, bile salt deficiency, SIBO)
    • post-mucosal (lymphatic obstruction: lymphoma, intestinal lymphangiectasia)
    • surface area loss (short bowel syndrome).

los.text: Link the function of the large bowel to its physiology and pathology.
los.html:
Functions
  • Absorption of water and electrolytes (concentrates ~1.5 L of ileal effluent to ~150 mL stool; Na⁺ absorption via ENaC (aldosterone), Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange, K⁺ secretion)
  • Fermentation of undigested carbohydrate by microbiota → short-chain fatty acids (butyrate: colonocyte fuel, anti-inflammatory) + gases
  • Storage and controlled evacuation of faeces
  • Mucus secretion (goblet cells).
Motility
  • Haustral segmentation (mixing, slow)
  • Mass movements (1–3/day, propel contents; triggered by gastrocolic reflex after meals)
  • Controlled by enteric nervous system (myenteric plexus; interstitial cells of Cajal as pacemakers)
  • Parasympathetic (vagus to splenic flexure; pelvic S2–4) ↑ motility
  • Sympathetic ↓.
Defecation
  • Rectal distension
  • → rectoanal inhibitory reflex (internal sphincter relaxes)
  • → sampling (anal canal sensation)
  • → voluntary external sphincter/puborectalis relaxation + Valsalva when appropriate.
Link to pathology
  • ↑ secretion/↓ absorption → diarrhoea (infection, colitis, bile acids, microscopic colitis).
  • ↓ motility → constipation (slow transit, opioids, hypothyroidism, Parkinson's), pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's).
  • Loss of ENS → Hirschsprung's disease, Chagas megacolon.
  • High intraluminal pressure (low fibre) → diverticula (sigmoid).
  • Hypokalaemia from colonic losses (diarrhoea, villous adenoma).
  • Microbiome disruption → C. difficile; dysbiosis in IBD/IBS.
  • Inflammation → colitis; colorectal cancer (adenoma–carcinoma sequence).

los.text: Apply knowledge of gastrointestinal symptoms and communication skills in a clinical setting to interpret the relevance of symptoms and guide differential diagnosis.
sessions: History taking in a polysymptomatic patient
los.html:
Approach to a polysymptomatic patient
  • Open questions
  • Let patient tell their story
  • Then systematically clarify each symptom (onset, duration, character, timing, relation to food/defaecation, aggravating/relieving, associated features, severity, impact)
  • SOCRATES for pain
  • Establish chronology (timeline) and which symptom matters most to the patient.
GI symptom relevance
  • Dysphagia (red flag: progressive, solids then liquids, weight loss → oesophageal cancer).
  • Dyspepsia/reflux, nausea/vomiting (bilious? obstruction), haematemesis/melaena (upper GI bleed).
  • Abdominal pain (site, colicky vs constant), bloating/distension.
  • Change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding (bright red vs dark, mixed), mucus, tenesmus, steatorrhoea.
  • Jaundice, pale stools/dark urine, pruritus.
  • Weight loss, anorexia, early satiety, night sweats, fatigue.
Communication skills
  • Signposting
  • Active listening
  • Summarising
  • ICE (ideas, concerns, expectations)
  • Acknowledging distress/frustration (multiple symptoms, prior investigations)
  • Validating experience
  • Avoiding premature closure or dismissing symptoms as "functional".
Use findings to narrow differentials (organic vs functional), prioritise red flags, and plan investigations.

los.text: Identify patterns in multiple symptoms to guide diagnostic thinking and integrate information from diverse symptoms to form a coherent clinical impression.
sessions: History taking in a polysymptomatic patient
los.html:
• Pattern recognition: group symptoms into syndromes rather than treating each in isolation.
Symptom clusterConsider
Diarrhoea + weight loss + anaemia + bloatingCoeliac disease, Crohn's, pancreatic insufficiency
Bloody diarrhoea + urgency + tenesmusIBD (UC), infective colitis
Abdominal pain relieved by defecation + bloating + altered habit, no red flagsIBS
Widespread pain + fatigue + IBS + poor sleep + headaches + low moodFibromyalgia / central sensitisation with overlapping functional disorders
Fatigue + weight gain + constipation + cold intoleranceHypothyroidism
Polyuria + thirst + weight loss + abdominal painDiabetes/DKA, hypercalcaemia
Joint pains + rash + mouth ulcers + diarrhoeaIBD with extraintestinal manifestations, SLE, coeliac
Weight loss + early satiety + dysphagia + anaemiaUpper GI malignancy
Flushing + diarrhoea + wheezeCarcinoid syndrome
Integrate
  • One diagnosis that explains most symptoms (Occam's razor) vs multiple coexisting conditions (Hickam's dictum: common in multimorbidity)
  • Consider psychosocial factors, medication side effects (polypharmacy), and somatic symptom presentations
  • Always check red flags.
Form a coherent impressionSummarise ("a 34-year-old woman with 2 years of ... suggestive of ...") with differential ranked by likelihood and seriousness.

los.text: Comprehend diagnostic criteria and pathophysiology of fibromyalgia, conveying this in lay terms to a patient.
sessions: History taking in a polysymptomatic patient
los.html:
Fibromyalgia
  • Chronic widespread pain (≥3 months) with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulties ("fibro fog"), often with IBS, headaches, mood disorders
  • ~2–5% population, women > men.
Diagnostic criteria (ACR 2010/2016)
  • Widespread Pain Index (WPI) ≥7 + Symptom Severity Scale (SSS) ≥5, or WPI 4–6 + SSS ≥9
  • Pain in ≥4 of 5 regions
  • Symptoms ≥3 months
  • The diagnosis is valid irrespective of other diagnoses.
  • (Old 1990 criteria used ≥11 of 18 tender points.)
Exclude
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica
  • Inflammatory arthritis
  • Myositis
  • Vitamin D deficiency
  • Anaemia → FBC
  • ESR/CRP
  • TFTs
  • CK
  • Calcium
  • Vitamin D
  • LFTs
  • U&E
  • HbA1c (normal in fibromyalgia).
Pathophysiology
  • Central sensitisation: the nervous system's "volume control" for pain is turned up (↑ excitatory neurotransmitters such as substance P/glutamate, ↓ descending inhibition (serotonin/noradrenaline)), abnormal pain processing on imaging
  • Triggers: stress, trauma, infection, sleep disturbance
  • Genetic predisposition.
Explaining in lay terms
  • "Your pain is real.
  • Tests show no damage to your joints or muscles; instead, the nerves and brain have become over-sensitive, like a car alarm that goes off too easily or a volume knob turned up too high.
  • That's why ordinary sensations can hurt and why you feel tired.
  • It's common
  • It won't damage your body
  • and there are things that can turn the volume down: gentle, gradually increased exercise
  • Good sleep habits
  • Pacing activities
  • and talking therapies.
  • Some medicines can help a little."
Management (NICE NG193 chronic primary pain)
  • Education, exercise programmes, CBT/ACT (acceptance and commitment therapy), acupuncture
  • Antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine, SSRIs) may help
  • Avoid opioids, gabapentinoids, NSAIDs, benzodiazepines (NICE: not recommended for chronic primary pain).

los.text: Elicit a focused gastrointestinal history, selecting relevant questions based on presenting symptoms
los.html:
• Presenting complaint then focused HPC by symptom (see ICM Year 2 › Gastrointestinal & liver › LO 1): pain (SOCRATES)
  • Vomiting (frequency, content: bile, blood ("coffee grounds"), faeculent)
  • Bowel habit (frequency, consistency (Bristol chart), blood, mucus, nocturnal)
  • Dysphagia
  • Dyspepsia
  • Jaundice
  • Weight loss.
Systems reviewFever, night sweats, anaemia symptoms, urinary symptoms, gynaecological (LMP, pregnancy, discharge), joint/skin/eye symptoms (IBD).
PMHPrevious GI disease (PUD, IBD, gallstones, pancreatitis), surgery (adhesions), liver disease, diabetes, thyroid.
Drug historyNSAIDs/aspirin, anticoagulants, PPIs, steroids, opioids, iron, antibiotics (C. diff), laxatives, metformin, herbal remedies, OTC.
Family historyBowel/upper GI cancer, IBD, coeliac, polyposis syndromes.
SocialAlcohol (units), smoking, diet, travel, occupation, recreational drugs (IV: hepatitis), sexual history (hepatitis), impact on life.
Select questions based on symptoms
  • e.g. jaundice → alcohol, drugs, IVDU, travel, tattoos, pale stools/dark urine, itching, pain (gallstones)
  • Dysphagia → progressive, level, weight loss, odynophagia, reflux history.

los.text: Demonstrate a structured gastrointestinal examination, identifying normal and abnormal findings
los.html:
Preparation
  • WIPER (Wash hands, Introduce, Permission/consent, Expose (nipples to knees, preserving dignity: usually nipples to symphysis), Reposition: lying flat, one pillow, arms by sides).
  • Ask about pain.
General inspectionJaundice, pallor, cachexia, distension, scars, stomas, drains, scratch marks, around bed (vomit bowls, stoma bags, feeding tubes).
HandsClubbing (IBD, cirrhosis, coeliac), leuconychia (hypoalbuminaemia), koilonychia (iron deficiency), palmar erythema, Dupuytren's, asterixis (hepatic flap), tremor.
ArmsBruising, scratch marks, spider naevi, track marks, AV fistula.
Face/neckScleral icterus, conjunctival pallor, xanthelasma, angular stomatitis, mouth ulcers, glossitis, dentition, parotid enlargement, Virchow's node (left supraclavicular: Troisier's sign), cervical nodes.
ChestSpider naevi (>5), gynaecomastia, loss of body hair.
Abdomen
  • Inspection: distension (fat, fluid, flatus, faeces, fetus), scars (name them), stomas, caput medusae, visible peristalsis, hernias.
  • Palpation: light then deep in 9 regions (watch face for pain; tenderness, guarding, rebound), masses; organs: liver (from RIF upwards with breathing), spleen (RIF → left costal margin; notch, can't get above), kidneys (ballot bimanually), AAA (expansile, pulsatile).
  • Percussion: liver span, spleen, bladder; shifting dullness (ascites) ± fluid thrill.
  • Auscultation: bowel sounds (absent: ileus; tinkling: obstruction), bruits (renal, aortic).
CompleteHernial orifices, external genitalia, DRE, urine dipstick, observations.

los.text: Perform a digital rectal examination safely, respectfully, and with appropriate consent
los.html:
Indications
  • Rectal bleeding
  • Change in bowel habit
  • Suspected prostate disease (LUTS, ↑PSA)
  • Constipation/impaction
  • Anal pain/mass
  • Faecal incontinence
  • Cord compression (anal tone)
  • Trauma (secondary survey)
  • Melaena assessment.
Consent and dignity
  • Explain why, what it involves, that it may be uncomfortable but shouldn't be painful
  • Verbal consent documented
  • Offer chaperone (document name or refusal)
  • Privacy (curtains, sheet covering)
  • Patient can stop at any time
  • Consider cultural/religious factors.
Procedure
  • Position: left lateral, knees drawn up to chest, buttocks at edge of bed.
  • Gloves + lubricant.
  • Inspect perianal area: skin tags, external haemorrhoids, fissures (posterior midline), fistulae, warts, ulcers, prolapse, blood, mucus, faeces, excoriation; ask patient to bear down.
  • Palpate: lubricated index finger placed flat over anus, wait for sphincter to relax, insert slowly towards umbilicus; assess anal tone (ask to squeeze), rectal walls (rotate 360° for masses, tenderness), prostate anteriorly in men (size, consistency (smooth/rubbery normal; hard/craggy), median sulcus, nodules, tenderness) or cervix/uterus in women; ask about sensation.
  • Withdraw, inspect glove (blood, melaena, mucus, stool colour).
  • Wipe patient, offer tissues, allow to dress in privacy.
DocumentConsent, chaperone, findings.

los.text: Summarise and communicate clinical findings concisely and clearly to colleagues
los.html:
Structure (SBAR or standard presentation)"I examined Mrs X, a 64-year-old woman presenting with ... On general inspection she appeared ... (comfortable/in pain, jaundiced, cachectic)."
  • Positive findings first, then pertinent negatives: "There were peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease including palmar erythema, multiple spider naevi and asterixis.
  • The abdomen was distended with shifting dullness, and there was 3 cm smooth, non-tender hepatomegaly.
  • No splenomegaly.
  • No signs of encephalopathy beyond asterixis."
Summary + impression
  • "These findings suggest decompensated chronic liver disease with ascites, likely secondary to ...
  • I would like to ...
  • (bloods incl. LFTs, INR, albumin; USS abdomen; diagnostic ascitic tap)."
Tips
  • Concise
  • Logical order
  • Avoid lists of normals
  • Use correct terms (e.g. "hepatomegaly 4 cm below costal margin in mid-clavicular line")
  • Quantify
  • Finish with differential and plan
  • SBAR for urgent handover (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)
  • Document clearly.

los.text: Formulate and justify a differential diagnosis using clinical reasoning and patient data
los.html:
Process
  • Gather data (history, exam, observations, bloods)
  • → identify key features (problem representation, e.g. "elderly man, iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss, change in bowel habit")
  • → generate differentials by anatomy/system and surgical sieve (VITAMIN CDEF: Vascular, Infective/Inflammatory, Trauma, Autoimmune, Metabolic, Iatrogenic, Neoplastic, Congenital, Degenerative, Endocrine, Functional)
  • → rank by likelihood and danger ("most likely" and "must not miss")
  • → choose tests that discriminate.
JustifyLink each differential to evidence for and against.
DifferentialForAgainst / next step
Colorectal cancer (most likely)Age, IDA, weight loss, change in habit, FHxColonoscopy
IBD (less likely)No diarrhoea/blood, normal CRP
CoeliacAnaemiaCheck tTG
Use probabilitiesPre-test probability, red flags, likelihood ratios of findings.
Avoid biasesAnchoring, premature closure, availability, confirmation bias; reconsider when new data arrive ("diagnostic time-out").
Example (RIF pain, young woman)Appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy (always β-hCG), ovarian torsion/cyst rupture, PID, mesenteric adenitis, Crohn's, UTI/pyelonephritis, renal colic.

los.text: Identify normal abdominal radiographic anatomy, including recognition of the four key densities (gas, fat, soft tissue, bone).
los.html:
Four key densities(from black to white)
  • Gas (black): bowel gas, free air.
  • Fat (dark grey): properitoneal fat lines, perirenal fat, psoas outlines.
  • Soft tissue/fluid (mid grey): liver, spleen, kidneys, bladder, muscles (psoas), bowel wall.
  • Bone/calcium (white): spine, pelvis, ribs, calcifications. (Plus metal brightest: clips, stents, prostheses.)
Normal anatomy
  • Gas pattern (stomach bubble, small bowel gas minimal, colonic gas with faeces in a peripheral "frame")
  • Liver (RUQ)
  • Spleen (LUQ)
  • Kidneys (T12–L3, lateral to psoas)
  • Psoas shadows
  • Bladder (pelvis)
  • Bones (lumbar spine, pelvis, hips, ribs, sacroiliac joints).
AXR indications (limited)
  • Suspected bowel obstruction, toxic megacolon (IBD), foreign bodies, renal stones (KUB), constipation (rarely).
  • Not for non-specific abdominal pain (CT preferred)
  • Erect CXR for perforation.
Radiation~0.7 mSv (≈ 35 CXRs).

los.text: Differentiate between small bowel and large bowel on radiographs using features such as valvulae conniventes, haustra, position, and presence of faeces
los.html:
FeatureSmall bowelLarge bowel
PositionCentralPeripheral ("picture frame")
FoldsValvulae conniventes (plicae circulares): thin, closely spaced, cross the entire width ("stack of coins")Haustra: thicker, widely spaced, don't cross the whole width
Diameter (upper normal)3 cm6 cm (9 cm caecum) — "3-6-9 rule"
ContentsGas/fluid; no faecesFaeces (mottled appearance)
Number of loopsManyFew
  • Small bowel loops are usually not visible on normal films (little gas) except in children.

los.text: Recognise radiographic signs of small bowel dilatation and large bowel dilatation, and relate these findings to underlying causes such as obstruction, ileus, or colitis
los.html:
Small bowel dilatation (>3 cm)
  • Multiple central dilated loops with valvulae conniventes; air–fluid levels (erect); "string of pearls" (gas trapped between folds).
  • Causes: mechanical obstruction: adhesions (commonest in developed countries; previous surgery), hernias (commonest worldwide; check orifices), tumours, Crohn's strictures, intussusception, gallstone ileus, volvulus; paralytic ileus (post-op, electrolytes (↓K⁺), opioids, peritonitis, pancreatitis).
Large bowel dilatation (>6 cm; caecum >9 cm)
  • Peripheral dilated loops with haustra.
  • Causes: colorectal cancer (commonest cause of LBO), volvulus (sigmoid, caecal), diverticular stricture, pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's) (no mechanical cause; elderly, post-op, sick), faecal impaction.
  • Toxic megacolon: transverse colon >6 cm with loss of haustra, mucosal oedema/"thumbprinting", in colitis (UC, C. difficile) with systemic toxicity → risk of perforation.
Obstruction vs ileus
  • Obstruction → dilated bowel proximal to a transition point with collapsed bowel distally
  • Ileus → gas throughout small and large bowel including rectum.
Closed loop obstruction(competent ileocaecal valve with LBO)Massive caecal dilatation → perforation risk.
Next stepCT abdomen/pelvis with contrast (cause, level, ischaemia, perforation).

los.text: Interpret radiological features of pneumoperitoneum, including Rigler’s sign and the presence of free air under the diaphragm.
los.html:
Pneumoperitoneum
  • Free intraperitoneal gas → usually perforated hollow viscus (perforated peptic ulcer, diverticulum, bowel tumour, obstruction) → surgical emergency.
  • Also normal for a few days post-laparotomy/laparoscopy, peritoneal dialysis.
Erect CXR(best plain film, patient upright ≥10 min)Free air under the diaphragm (crescent of gas between diaphragm and liver; under left hemidiaphragm don't confuse with gastric bubble/Chilaiditi sign (colon between liver and diaphragm: haustra visible)).
Supine AXR signs
  • Rigler's sign (double wall sign): both sides of the bowel wall visible (gas inside and outside lumen) → wall appears as a thin white line.
  • Football sign: large oval lucency over abdomen (large volume).
  • Falciform ligament sign: ligament outlined by gas.
  • Triangle sign: triangular gas between loops.
  • Lucent liver sign; gas outlining the lesser sac.
CT is most sensitive (small volumes, site of perforation).
ManagementResuscitation, NBM, IV antibiotics, analgesia, urgent surgical review (laparotomy/laparoscopy); conservative in selected (sealed perforation).

los.text: Describe the common causes and appearances of abnormal calcifications (renal calculi, gallstones, bladder stones, vascular calcifications, and staghorn calculi)
los.html:
CalcificationAppearance/locationNotes
Renal calculiDense opacities over renal outlines/along ureters (tips of transverse processes → SIJ → bladder)~90% radio-opaque (calcium), urate radiolucent; confirm with CT KUB
Staghorn calculusLarge branching stone filling the renal pelvis and calyces (shape of a stag's antlers)Struvite (Proteus, urease) ± cystine; needs PCNL
GallstonesRUQ, often faceted/laminated ringsOnly ~10–15% radio-opaque; USS is test of choice; porcelain gallbladder
Bladder stonesRounded/laminated opacity in the pelvis midlineStasis (BPH, neurogenic bladder), infection, schistosomiasis
Vascular calcification
  • Linear "tram-track" or curvilinear lines: aorta, iliac and splenic arteries
  • AAA (curvilinear outline of aneurysm), phleboliths (small round pelvic vein calcifications with lucent centre: normal, mistaken for ureteric stones)
Other
  • Pancreatic calcification (chronic pancreatitis, speckled across upper abdomen)
  • Calcified lymph nodes (mesenteric, TB)
  • Fibroids (popcorn)
  • Costal cartilage
  • Appendicolith (faecolith in RIF)
  • Adrenal calcification (TB/old haemorrhage)
  • Nephrocalcinosis (medullary sponge kidney, hyperparathyroidism)

los.text: Explain the radiographic appearances and clinical implications of common abdominal emergencies, such as volvulus, toxic megacolon, perforation, and gallstone ileus
los.html:
EmergencyAXR appearanceClinical implications
Sigmoid volvulusMassively dilated loop "coffee bean" sign arising from pelvis pointing to RUQ, loss of haustra, no rectal gasElderly, constipated, institutionalised; flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression + flatus tube; surgery if ischaemia/recurrent
Caecal volvulusDilated caecum displaced to left upper/central abdomen ("embryo/comma" shape), dilated small bowelYounger; surgery (right hemicolectomy)
Toxic megacolonTransverse colon >6 cm, loss of haustra, thumbprinting, mucosal islandsUC/C. difficile; IV steroids/antibiotics, urgent surgical review, colectomy if no improvement or perforation
PerforationFree gas: Rigler's sign, football sign; erect CXR free air under diaphragmLaparotomy; sepsis management
Gallstone ileusRigler's triad: small bowel obstruction + pneumobilia (gas in biliary tree) + ectopic gallstone (often RIF)Elderly women; cholecystoduodenal fistula; stone impacts at terminal ileum; surgery (enterolithotomy)
Small/large bowel obstructionSee LO 27Drip and suck (NG + IV fluids) vs surgery
Ischaemic bowelThumbprinting, pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in bowel wall), portal venous gas (late, grave)CT angiography, surgery
  • CT is now the main investigation for most acute abdomens; AXR is a quick first look.

los.text: Apply a systematic approach to abdominal radiograph interpretation that integrates clinical information with imaging findings
los.html:
• Systematic approach:
1Patient details, date, projection (supine AP standard; erect rarely), quality, previous films ("old is gold").
2. Bowel gas patternSmall vs large bowel (LO 26), calibre (3-6-9 rule), distribution, transition point, rectal gas, wall thickening/thumbprinting, pneumatosis.
3. Extraluminal gasPneumoperitoneum (Rigler's), pneumobilia (post-ERCP/sphincterotomy or fistula), portal venous gas, retroperitoneal gas.
4. Soft tissues/solid organsLiver, spleen, kidneys, bladder size, psoas outlines (loss: retroperitoneal process), masses.
5. BonesSpine, pelvis, hips, ribs (fractures, metastases (lytic/sclerotic), Paget's, sacroiliitis).
6Calcifications (LO 29) and artefacts/devices (clips, stents, IUCD, lines, foreign bodies).
Integrate clinically
  • e.g. vomiting + distension + absolute constipation + previous laparotomy + dilated small bowel = adhesional SBO
  • Elderly with constipation + coffee bean = sigmoid volvulus
  • Colitis patient with fever + dilated transverse colon = toxic megacolon.
Act
  • Next imaging (CT), surgical referral, resuscitation
  • Document report: "This is a supine AXR of ...
  • The most striking abnormality is ...
  • In summary ...".

los.text: Identify the caecum, vermiform appendix, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal, and be able to name the appropriate arterial and nervous supplies and venous and lymphatic drainage. Note their position in the living and that the colic arteries form an anastomosis.
los.html:
RegionArterial supplyVenous drainageLymphNerves
Caecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal ⅔ transverse colon (midgut)SMA: ileocolic (→ appendicular), right colic, middle colicSMV → portal veinSuperior mesenteric nodesSympathetic (T10–T12, lesser splanchnic); vagus
Distal ⅓ transverse, descending, sigmoid colon, upper rectum (hindgut)IMA: left colic, sigmoid arteries, superior rectalIMV → splenic vein → portalInferior mesenteric nodesSympathetic (L1–L2, lumbar splanchnic); pelvic splanchnic (S2–4) parasympathetic
Rectum (middle/lower)Superior rectal (IMA), middle rectal (internal iliac), inferior rectalSuperior rectal → portal; middle/inferior rectal → systemic (portosystemic anastomosis)Pararectal → inferior mesenteric / internal iliac
Anal canal above pectinate lineSuperior rectalPortalInternal iliacAutonomic (visceral: insensitive to pain)
Anal canal below pectinate lineInferior rectal (internal pudendal)Systemic (internal iliac via pudendal)Superficial inguinal nodesInferior rectal (pudendal) nerve: somatic (painful)
Marginal artery (of Drummond)
  • Anastomosis along the colon connecting SMA and IMA branches
  • Watershed areas: splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and rectosigmoid (Sudeck's point) → ischaemic colitis.
Position in living
  • Caecum in RIF, appendix base at McBurney's point
  • Ascending colon right flank
  • Transverse colon hanging variably (can reach pelvis)
  • Descending left flank
  • Sigmoid LIF/pelvis
  • Rectum anterior to sacrum (S3 to anorectal junction).

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the appendix and the significance of its variations in relation to appendicitis
los.html:
Appendix
  • 6–10 cm blind tube from the posteromedial caecum ~2 cm below ileocaecal valve
  • Taeniae coli converge at its base (surgical landmark)
  • Has its own mesentery (mesoappendix) carrying the appendicular artery (branch of ileocolic; end artery → obstruction leads to gangrene/perforation)
  • Rich lymphoid tissue (peaks in teens: why appendicitis is commonest in young people).
Surface marking of baseMcBurney's point (⅓ of the way from ASIS to umbilicus).
Positional variations of the tip(base is constant)
  • Retrocaecal (~65%): commonest; may lack peritonism anteriorly; flank/back pain; psoas sign (pain on hip extension).
  • Pelvic (~30%): suprapubic pain, urinary frequency/dysuria, diarrhoea/tenesmus (irritates rectum), tenderness on PR; obturator sign (pain on internal rotation of flexed hip).
  • Subcaecal, pre-ileal, post-ileal (vague pain, vomiting, diarrhoea).
  • Pregnancy: displaced upwards (RUQ pain in 3rd trimester).
  • Malrotation/situs inversus: left-sided.
Significance
  • Atypical presentations (delayed diagnosis → perforation), differential diagnoses mimic it, surgical approach
  • Visceral pain first periumbilical (midgut: T10) → somatic pain in RIF once parietal peritoneum inflamed.

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the ischio-anal/rectal fossa and explain its potential involvement in abscesses, anal glands and fissures.
los.html:
Ischioanal (ischiorectal) fossa
  • Wedge-shaped, fat-filled space on each side of the anal canal in the anal triangle of the perineum.
  • Boundaries: medial: levator ani and external anal sphincter; lateral: obturator internus (and its fascia) and ischium; superior (apex): origin of levator ani from obturator fascia; inferior (base): perianal skin; anterior: perineal membrane/urogenital diaphragm (anterior recesses extend forwards above it); posterior: sacrotuberous ligament and gluteus maximus.
  • Contents: ischioanal fat (allows anal canal distension), pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) on lateral wall (contains internal pudendal vessels and pudendal nerve), inferior rectal vessels and nerves crossing the fossa, lymphatics.
  • The two fossae communicate posteriorly behind the anal canal (horseshoe abscess can spread from one side to the other).
Anal glands
  • Open into anal crypts at the pectinate line
  • May extend into the internal sphincter/intersphincteric plane → cryptoglandular infection → perianal/ischioanal abscesses → fistula-in-ano (Goodsall's rule).
Abscess typesPerianal (commonest), ischioanal (large, deep, painful; buttock swelling, fever), intersphincteric, supralevator.
Anal fissure
  • Tear in anoderm below pectinate line, usually posterior midline (poor blood supply, high pressure)
  • Very painful (somatic innervation)
  • Internal sphincter spasm
  • Rx: GTN/diltiazem ointment, botox, sphincterotomy.

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the sigmoid colon and rectum and their anatomical relationships.
los.html:
Sigmoid colon
  • From pelvic brim (end of descending colon) to S3 (rectosigmoid junction), ~40 cm
  • Intraperitoneal, mobile on its sigmoid mesocolon (inverted V root over left ureter and iliac vessel bifurcation) → volvulus risk
  • Site of diverticula and cancers.
  • Relations: bladder (men) / uterus (women), ileal loops, left ureter, left external iliac vessels, left ovary.
Rectum(~12–15 cm)
  • From S3 to the anorectal junction (puborectalis sling)
  • No taeniae (spread into continuous longitudinal muscle), no mesentery/appendices epiploicae
  • Lateral curvatures with transverse rectal folds (valves of Houston)
  • Ampulla stores faeces.
  • Peritoneum: upper ⅓ covered anteriorly and laterally, middle ⅓ anteriorly only, lower ⅓ extraperitoneal.
  • Mesorectum: fat containing vessels and lymph nodes enclosed by mesorectal fascia (total mesorectal excision in rectal cancer).
  • Relations: posterior: sacrum, coccyx, median sacral vessels, sacral plexus, sympathetic trunk; anterior (male): rectovesical pouch, bladder, seminal vesicles, vas deferens, prostate (palpable on DRE), separated by Denonvilliers' fascia; anterior (female): rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), uterus, cervix, posterior vaginal wall (rectovaginal septum); lateral: pararectal fossae, levator ani, ureters.
Clinical
  • DRE palpates prostate/cervix, pouch of Douglas (pelvic abscess, metastatic deposits: "Blumer's shelf")
  • Rectal cancer spread
  • Damage to pelvic autonomic nerves in surgery (sexual/bladder dysfunction).

los.text: Identify the internal anal sphincter and the insertion of levator ani into the lateral wall of the anal canal and the pubo-rectalis part of the muscle which passes round the posterior wall.
los.html:
Internal anal sphincter (IAS)
  • Thickened continuation of the inner circular smooth muscle of the rectum, surrounding the upper ~⅔ of the anal canal
  • Involuntary
  • Sympathetic tone keeps it contracted
  • Relaxes with rectal distension (rectoanal inhibitory reflex).
Levator ani(pelvic diaphragm)
  • Iliococcygeus, pubococcygeus, puborectalis
  • Arises from the body of pubis, tendinous arch of obturator internus fascia, ischial spine
  • Inserts into the perineal body, anococcygeal ligament, coccyx and blends with the lateral wall of the anal canal (conjoint longitudinal muscle passes between internal and external sphincters).
Puborectalis
  • Medial part of levator ani from the back of the pubic bodies, forms a U-shaped sling around the posterior wall of the anorectal junction → pulls it forward creating the anorectal angle (~90°) important for continence
  • Relaxes and the angle straightens during defaecation.
InnervationLevator ani: nerve to levator ani (S4) and pudendal branches; puborectalis: S3–4 and pudendal.
Identify in specimens/imagingIAS as the inner thickened smooth muscle ring; external sphincter outside; puborectalis sling at the anorectal junction behind.

los.text: Explain the functional anatomy of the anal sphincters and their role in faecal continence.
los.html:
Components
  • Internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle, involuntary): provides ~70–85% of resting anal pressure; tonic sympathetic contraction; relaxes reflexly with rectal distension (RAIR).
  • External anal sphincter (skeletal, voluntary; inferior rectal branch of pudendal nerve, S2–4): subcutaneous, superficial, deep parts; maintains squeeze pressure; contracts voluntarily to defer defaecation and reflexly with ↑ abdominal pressure (cough).
  • Puborectalis: maintains the anorectal angle (flap valve); continuous tonic contraction.
  • Anal cushions (vascular): contribute ~15% of resting pressure; fine seal for gas/liquid.
  • Rectal compliance and sensation: rectum accommodates stool; awareness of filling.
  • Anal sensation (somatic, below pectinate line): "sampling reflex" distinguishes gas/liquid/solid.
Continence mechanism
  • Rectal filling
  • → sensation of urge
  • → RAIR (IAS relaxes)
  • → sampling
  • → if inappropriate: voluntary contraction of EAS and puborectalis pushes contents back (rectum accommodates)
  • → urge passes.
  • Defaecation: relax EAS/puborectalis (straighten angle) + Valsalva.
Incontinence causes
  • Obstetric sphincter injury (3rd/4th degree tears; pudendal nerve stretch)
  • Surgery (fistulotomy, sphincterotomy)
  • Neurological (spinal cord injury, cauda equina, MS, diabetes, dementia)
  • Diarrhoea
  • Faecal impaction with overflow
  • Rectal prolapse
  • Ageing.

los.text: Explain that most of the anal canal is in the perineum, not the pelvis.
los.html:
Anal canal(~4 cm)From the anorectal junction (where the rectum passes through the pelvic diaphragm/levator ani, at the puborectalis sling) to the anal verge.
  • Because it begins below the pelvic floor, almost all of the anal canal lies in the anal triangle of the perineum, not in the pelvic cavity
  • Surrounded by the ischioanal fossae laterally and the sphincter complex.
Implications
  • Its lower part has somatic innervation (pudendal/inferior rectal nerves) and inguinal lymph drainage
  • Perianal and ischioanal sepsis is a perineal problem (abscesses track in perineal spaces)
  • Surgical approaches to anal lesions are perineal
  • Rectal tumours vs anal tumours behave and spread differently (anal SCC → inguinal nodes; rectal adenocarcinoma → mesorectal/internal iliac nodes).
Pectinate (dentate) line
  • Watershed between endoderm (above: columnar epithelium, visceral innervation, portal drainage, internal iliac lymph) and ectoderm (below: stratified squamous, somatic, systemic veins, superficial inguinal lymph)
  • Anal columns (of Morgagni) and valves/crypts here.

los.text: Describe the blood supply and venous drainage of the distal bowel; the supply from the superior rectal (inferior mesenteric), middle rectal (internal iliac) and inferior rectal arteries (from pudendal to anal canal only), and portal-systemic venous anastomosis.
los.html:
Arterial supply
  • Superior rectal artery: continuation of the IMA; main supply of rectum and upper anal canal (above pectinate line).
  • Middle rectal arteries: from internal iliac; supply lower rectum/muscle; anastomose.
  • Inferior rectal arteries: from internal pudendal (internal iliac) via pudendal canal, cross ischioanal fossa; supply anal canal below pectinate line and sphincters.
  • Median sacral artery (minor).
Venous drainage
  • Superior rectal vein → IMV → splenic vein → portal system.
  • Middle and inferior rectal veins → internal iliac/internal pudendal → systemic (IVC).
  • Rich internal rectal venous plexus (submucosa; forms anal cushions) and external plexus connect the systems → portosystemic anastomosis.
Clinical
  • in portal hypertension, these anastomoses dilate → rectal (anorectal) varices (distinct from haemorrhoids)
  • Rectal cancer spreads via portal (liver mets) and systemic (lungs) routes
  • Rectally administered drugs partially bypass first-pass metabolism (lower rectum → systemic).

los.text: Describe the vascular anal cushions and explain their role in continence
los.html:
Anal cushions
  • Three submucosal vascular cushions in the upper anal canal.
  • Position: 3, 7 and 11 o'clock in lithotomy (left lateral, right posterior, right anterior).
  • Contents: AV communications (sinusoids) from superior rectal vessels, smooth muscle (Treitz's), connective tissue.
Role in continence
  • Act like a compressible seal that completes closure of the anal canal → contribute ~15–20% of resting anal pressure
  • Provide fine control of gas and liquid
  • Protect sphincters during defaecation
  • Engorge when straining/coughing.
HaemorrhoidsPathological enlargement/prolapse of the cushions (straining, constipation, pregnancy, low fibre, ageing).
InternalExternal
SiteAbove pectinate lineBelow pectinate line
SymptomsPainless bright red bleeding on paper/panPainful when thrombosed
GradingI–IV by prolapse
  • Clinical: haemorrhoidectomy may slightly impair continence (loss of cushions)
    • management: fibre/fluids, topical treatments, rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, haemorrhoidal artery ligation, surgery.

los.text: Recognise the regions of the large intestine on radiographs
los.html:
Plain AXR
  • Colon identified by peripheral position ("frame"), haustral folds (incomplete across lumen), faecal material (mottled)
  • Caecum (RIF, largest calibre)
  • Ascending colon (right flank)
  • Hepatic flexure (under liver)
  • Transverse colon (variable, across upper abdomen, can sag to pelvis)
  • Splenic flexure (LUQ, higher than hepatic)
  • Descending colon (left flank, often gasless/narrow)
  • Sigmoid (LIF/pelvis, redundant loops)
  • Rectum (midline pelvis, gas often visible in the rectum on normal films).
Contrast studies
  • Barium/water-soluble enema (outline colon: "apple-core" stricture = carcinoma)
  • CT colonography ("virtual colonoscopy")
  • CT abdomen/pelvis (colon wall, pericolic fat, diverticula, masses)
  • MRI pelvis (rectal cancer staging: mesorectal fascia).
AppendixAppendicolith on AXR (RIF calcification); USS (dilated non-compressible tube >6 mm) or CT.
Key abnormalitiesDilated colon (obstruction, volvulus, pseudo-obstruction), toxic megacolon, faecal loading, lead-pipe colon (chronic UC: loss of haustra), diverticula on CT/barium.
